title: Frankenstein
author: Mary Shelley
ru: Молодой учёный создаёт живое существо, отвергает его — и чудовище, жаждущее любви, начинает мстить создателю

chapters.title: Chapter 1. A Stranger on the Ice
chapters.text:
St. Petersburg, 11th December.

My dear Margaret,

You will be glad to hear that I have arrived here safely, and that nothing has gone wrong with the plan you always feared so much. As I walk through the streets of this city, a cold northern wind blows against my face. It comes from the place I am going to, and strangely, it fills me with hope.

You know my dream. Since I was a boy I have wanted to sail to the North Pole, to a land no human being has ever seen. Perhaps I will find a sea passage across the top of the world. Perhaps I will learn the secret of the strange power that pulls every compass needle north. Whatever happens, I will set my foot where no one has stepped before. Is that not worth a few years of danger and cold?

I have hired a ship and a crew of brave, experienced men. Only one thing is missing, and I feel it more every day: I have no friend. There is no one on board who shares my dreams, no one to read with, no one to tell me when I am wrong. You will laugh at your romantic brother, but I am lonely.

On the ice, 5th August.

My dear sister,

We sailed from Archangel at the end of June, and for weeks we have been pushing further north. Now something so strange has happened that I must write it down at once, although you may never read these pages.

Last Monday our ship was almost completely surrounded by ice, and a thick fog lay all around us. We could do nothing but wait. At about two o'clock the fog cleared, and we saw great plains of ice stretching in every direction, without end. Some of my men groaned, and I was beginning to feel anxious myself, when a strange sight caught our attention.

About half a mile away, a sledge pulled by dogs was racing towards the north. In it sat a figure shaped like a man, but of enormous size. We watched him through our telescopes until he disappeared among the distant hills of ice. Nobody said a word. We were hundreds of miles from any land, and yet here was a traveller. And what a traveller!

During the night the ice broke up. In the morning I found my sailors leaning over the side of the ship, talking to someone below. A large piece of ice had floated close to us, and on it lay another sledge, with only one living dog. Beside it was a man. He was not a giant like the other one. He was an ordinary European, and he was half frozen.

“Here is our captain,” one of the sailors called down to him. “He won't let you die out here.”

The stranger looked up at me and spoke in English, with a foreign accent. “Before I come on board your ship,” he said, “will you kindly tell me where you are going?”

Imagine my surprise! A man on the edge of death, and he wanted to know our destination, as if he might refuse our help. I told him we were sailing north, towards the Pole. Only then did he agree to come on board.

Margaret, I have never seen anyone in such a terrible state. His hands and feet were nearly frozen, and he was as thin as a skeleton. We carried him to my cabin, rubbed him with brandy and gave him hot soup. For two days he could hardly speak.

When he was a little stronger, my lieutenant asked him why he had come so far across the ice in such a strange vehicle. A deep sadness came over his face.

“To look for one who ran away from me,” he said.

“Did the man you are chasing travel in the same way?”

“Yes.”

“Then I think we saw him. The day before we found you, a sledge with a man in it crossed the ice.”

The stranger sat up at once. He asked a hundred questions about the route the giant had taken. Since then, whenever he has the strength, he goes on deck and watches the ice for hours.

13th August.

I am beginning to love this man like a brother. He is gentle and wise, and when he talks about books or nature, his words are beautiful. Yet some terrible sorrow lies on him, and he seems to carry it everywhere, like a heavy coat he cannot take off.

Last night I told him about my own dream, and how gladly I would give my life to gain the knowledge I was searching for. As I spoke, a dark shadow passed over his face. He covered his eyes with his hands, and I saw tears running between his fingers.

“Unhappy man!” he cried. “Do you share my madness? Have you drunk from the same poisoned cup? Listen to me. Let me tell you my story, and then decide for yourself.”

He was silent for a long time. Then he looked at me with strange, burning eyes.

“You are looking for knowledge, as I once did,” he said. “I hope that when you find it, it does not turn into a snake and bite you, as it bit me. Tomorrow, if I am still alive, I will begin. My name is Victor Frankenstein.”

chapters.title: Chapter 2. The Boy Who Wanted to Know Everything
chapters.text:
I was born in Geneva, into one of the most respected families of that city. My father, Alphonse Frankenstein, had spent his life in public service, and everyone trusted him. My mother, Caroline, was much younger than he was, and they loved each other deeply. I was their first child, and for years their only one. They treated me like a precious toy that heaven had lent them.

When I was about five, my mother visited a poor family on the shores of Lake Como, in Italy. Among their hungry, dark-haired children she noticed a little girl who looked completely different: fair-haired, blue-eyed, as delicate as a flower. Her name was Elizabeth. She was an orphan, and the poor family had been caring for her out of kindness. My mother asked if she could take the child home, and so Elizabeth came to live with us.

“I have a pretty present for my Victor,” my mother said on the day she arrived. I took her words literally. From that moment, I thought of Elizabeth as mine, a gift to protect and love. She was calm and gentle where I was hot-tempered and restless. While I wanted to understand the world, she was content simply to admire it.

My closest friend was Henry Clerval, the son of a Geneva merchant. Henry loved stories of knights and heroes, and he wrote little plays in which we all had to act. Later my two younger brothers were born, Ernest and little William. No childhood could have been happier than mine.

And yet, even then, something in me was hungry. I did not care about languages or laws. I wanted to know the secrets of heaven and earth: what things are made of, and what makes them live.

When I was thirteen, our family spent a rainy day at an inn, and there I found an old book by Cornelius Agrippa, a sixteenth-century magician who claimed to know the secrets of nature. I read it with growing excitement and ran to show my father.

He glanced at the title. “Ah, Cornelius Agrippa! My dear Victor, don't waste your time on this. It's sad rubbish.”

If he had explained why it was rubbish, I would probably have thrown the book away. But he did not explain, and so I read it again, and then everything else I could find by Agrippa and other old alchemists. I dreamed of discovering the elixir of life, a drink that would protect the human body from every disease. What glory, if I could make a man who could never die!

When I was fifteen, I watched a violent thunderstorm from the doorway of our house. Suddenly a stream of fire shot out of the sky and struck an old oak tree about twenty yards away. When the light disappeared, the oak had vanished. Nothing remained but a black, smoking stump. A scientist who was staying with us explained electricity to me that evening, and I was amazed. Here was a power that could destroy a tree in a second. What else could it do?

At seventeen, I was sent to the University of Ingolstadt, in Germany. But before I left, the first misfortune of my life arrived. Elizabeth caught scarlet fever. My mother would not leave her bedside, and Elizabeth recovered, but my mother caught the disease herself. On her deathbed she joined my hand with Elizabeth's.

“My children,” she said, “my greatest hope was to see you married one day. Now that hope must comfort your father.” A few days later she was dead.

I left for Ingolstadt with a heavy heart. At the university I first visited Professor Krempe, a short, rough man with a sour face. When I told him what I had been reading, he stared at me.

“Have you really spent your time on such nonsense?” he said. “Every minute you have given to those books is completely lost. You must begin your studies all over again.”

I disliked him at once. But a few days later I heard a lecture by Professor Waldman, a kind, grey-haired man with a voice I will never forget.

“The old masters promised impossible things and achieved nothing,” he said. “Modern scientists promise very little. Their hands seem made only to dig in dirt, and their eyes only to look through a microscope. And yet they have performed real miracles. They have discovered how the blood moves through the body, and what the air we breathe is made of. They can command the thunder of heaven itself.”

As he spoke, I felt as if my soul were being played like a musical instrument. One by one, its strings were touched, and soon my whole mind was filled with a single thought.

So much has been done, I said to myself. But I will do far more. I will follow the path others have opened, and then go further than any of them. I will explore unknown powers and show the world the deepest secret of creation.

I did not know then that I was walking towards my own destruction.

chapters.title: Chapter 3. A Dreary Night in November
chapters.text:
From that day, science became my whole life. I went to Professor Waldman's lectures and to his laboratory, and I read day and night. Two years passed, and I did not once go home to Geneva.

Then one question began to fill my mind. Where does life come from? What is the spark that turns dead matter into a living, breathing creature?

To understand life, I first had to study death. I learned anatomy, but that was not enough. I spent days and nights in burial vaults and in the cold rooms where bodies were kept. I watched how the fine shape of a human being decays, how the bright eye and the strong arm become food for worms. Another man might have felt horror. I felt only curiosity.

And then, after months of exhausting work, a sudden light broke over me. It was so brilliant and yet so simple that I was amazed no one had seen it before. I had discovered the cause of life. More than that: I was now able to give life to lifeless matter.

You are looking at me with eager eyes, Walton. I can see that you hope I will tell you the secret. I will not. Learn from me, if not from my words, then from my example, how dangerous knowledge can be, and how much happier is the man who believes his own town is the whole world than the man who wants to become greater than nature allows.

For a long time I could not decide what kind of creature to make. At last I chose to make a human being. The small parts of the body were difficult to work with, so I decided to make him very large: about eight feet tall, with a body to match. I collected my materials from graveyards and from the dissecting rooms of the university, and sometimes from the slaughterhouse. I worked in a small room at the top of the house, which I called my workshop of filthy creation. My eyes ached, my hands shook, and my cheeks grew pale. I hardly noticed. Summer came and went, the most beautiful summer in years, and I did not see it. My father's letters lay unanswered on my table.

It was on a dreary night of November that I saw my work completed. It was already one in the morning, and the rain was beating on the windows. My candle was nearly burnt out. I gathered my instruments around me and put the spark of life into the thing that lay at my feet. By the faint, half-dead light I saw the dull yellow eye of the creature open. It breathed hard, and a violent movement shook its arms and legs.

How can I describe what I felt? I had chosen every feature for its beauty. Beauty! Great God! His yellow skin hardly covered the muscles and arteries beneath. His hair was black and flowing, and his teeth were as white as pearls, but these only made the rest more horrible: his watery eyes, almost the same colour as their pale sockets, his wrinkled face and his straight black lips.

For nearly two years I had worked for this moment. Now that it had come, the beauty of my dream disappeared, and my heart was filled with horror and disgust. I could not bear to look at what I had made. I rushed out of the room and threw myself onto my bed, still in my clothes.

At last I fell asleep, and I dreamed. I saw Elizabeth walking in the streets of Ingolstadt, healthy and lovely. I kissed her, but as my lips touched hers, they turned the colour of death. She changed, and I was holding the body of my dead mother, with worms crawling in the folds of the cloth she had been buried in.

I woke up shaking, cold sweat on my forehead. And there, by the yellow light of the moon, I saw him. The wretch, the miserable monster I had created, was holding up the curtain of my bed. His eyes, if they can be called eyes, were fixed on me. His jaws opened, and he made some sounds I could not understand, while a grin spread across his face. One hand was stretched out, as if to hold me, but I escaped and ran down the stairs.

I spent the rest of the night in the courtyard, listening to every sound, afraid that each one announced the arrival of the demon I had brought to life.

In the morning I walked the wet streets without knowing where I was going. Near an inn, a coach stopped, and a familiar voice called my name. It was Henry Clerval! His father had finally allowed him to study at the university. I was so glad to see him that for a moment I forgot everything. But when we reached my rooms, I made Henry wait outside while I opened the door. My heart was pounding.

The room was empty. My terrible guest had gone.

I laughed wildly and clapped my hands, and Henry stared at me in alarm. Then, suddenly, I fell to the floor. It was the start of a nervous fever that kept me in bed for months. Through all that time, the monster's face never left my dreams.

chapters.title: Chapter 4. Lightning Over the Lake
chapters.text:
Henry nursed me through that long winter with the patience of a brother. He told my family nothing about how ill I was, because he knew the news would break my father's heart. When at last I began to recover, spring had come. I could look at the green leaves outside my window again, and Henry gave me a letter from Elizabeth, which had waited for weeks on my table.

She wrote about ordinary things: little William's games, my father's health, and our servant Justine Moritz, a sweet, cheerful girl who had lived with us for years and whom we all loved like a member of the family. Reading those simple lines, I felt almost happy. Henry and I spent the following weeks walking in the countryside, and I began to plan my return home.

Then another letter came. It was from my father.

“Victor,” he wrote, “William is dead. That sweet child, whose smile delighted all of us, has been murdered.”

He explained what had happened. One warm evening the family had gone for a walk near Plainpalais, outside Geneva. William had run ahead to hide, as a game, and he did not come back. They searched for him all night. In the morning my father found him lying in the grass, pale and still. The marks of a murderer's fingers were on his neck.

That same evening, William had begged Elizabeth to let him wear a small, valuable picture of our mother. The picture had disappeared. The murderer, it seemed, had killed the child to steal it.

I left for Geneva at once. When I arrived, it was night, and the city gates were already closed. So I decided to spend the night in the village of Sécheron and walk to the place where William had been killed. A storm was coming over the mountains. As I walked, the thunder grew louder and the lightning lit up the lake, making it look like a great sheet of fire.

“William, dear angel!” I cried aloud. “This is your funeral.”

At that moment I saw a figure in the darkness, behind a clump of trees. I stood still and stared. A flash of lightning lit up the figure, and I saw its gigantic size and its horrible face. It was the wretch, the filthy demon to whom I had given life.

What was he doing here? Then a thought struck me with the force of the lightning itself. He was the murderer of my brother. I had no doubt at all.

I wanted to chase him, but another flash showed him climbing the almost vertical rocks of Mont Salève, a mountain near the city. He moved faster than any man could, and in a moment he was gone.

I could not tell anyone what I knew. Who would believe a story about a creature built from dead bodies, which had come to life in my room? They would think I had gone mad, and perhaps they would be right.

At home I found my father aged by grief and Elizabeth pale with tears. Ernest met me at the door with more news.

“Victor, since Father wrote to you, we have found out who the murderer is.”

“You have found him?” I cried. “Impossible! Nobody could catch him. You might as well try to catch the wind.”

Ernest looked at me strangely. “I don't know what you mean. It was Justine.”

The picture of my mother had been found in the pocket of her dress. She had been out on the night of the murder, searching for William, and had spent the night in a barn. She could not explain how the picture came to be in her pocket.

“She is innocent,” I said. “I know she is innocent.” But I could say nothing more.

Her trial took place the next day. Justine stood in front of the judges, calm and dressed in mourning, and told the truth as simply as a child. Elizabeth spoke for her bravely and described how kind Justine had always been, and how she had loved William as if he were her own son. It was no use. The evidence was too strong, and the crowd had already decided she was guilty.

Worse was to come. While she was in prison, a priest threatened her with hell until, terrified and confused, Justine confessed to a crime she had not committed. When Elizabeth and I visited her in her cell, she wept in Elizabeth's arms.

“I confessed a lie,” she said, “and now I feel more miserable than ever. But I am ready to die. God knows I am innocent.”

I sat in a corner of that cell, and inside me was a pain far worse than hers. She, at least, was innocent. The guilt of everything was eating at my heart, and I could not say a word.

The next morning Justine was hanged.

William and Justine were the first victims of my experiment. And I knew, with terrible certainty, that they would not be the last.

chapters.title: Chapter 5. The Meeting on the Glacier
chapters.text:
After Justine's death, I could not rest. Sleep would not come, and in the daytime I wandered like a ghost. Sometimes, on long nights, I took a boat out alone onto the lake and let it drift in the darkness. More than once I looked down into the black water and thought how easy it would be to end everything. Only the thought of Elizabeth and my old father, left alone with that monster still loose in the world, stopped me.

I hated the creature with a hatred I had never known before. I dreamed of meeting him again, so that I could destroy him.

In August, my father suggested a journey to the valley of Chamonix, at the foot of Mont Blanc, hoping the mountains would heal us. In a way, they did. The enormous glaciers and the white peaks rising above the clouds made my own suffering feel small. For a few hours at a time, I could almost forget.

One morning I decided to climb Montanvert alone and look at the great glacier called the Mer de Glace, the Sea of Ice. By noon I reached the top. Below me, the ice spread out like a frozen ocean, its surface broken into waves and deep cracks.

Suddenly I saw a figure some distance away, coming towards me at an incredible speed. He leapt over the cracks in the ice that I had crossed so carefully. As he came closer, I saw that he was taller than any man. My legs went weak and a mist came over my eyes. It was him: the creature I had made.

I trembled with rage and horror. I decided to wait for him and fight to the death.

“Devil!” I shouted. “How dare you come near me? Aren't you afraid that I'll take my revenge? Go away, you disgusting insect! Or rather, stay, so that I can crush you into the dust!”

He looked at me calmly. His face showed bitter sorrow and something like contempt.

“I expected this,” he said. His voice was deep, and he spoke clearly and beautifully. “All men hate the wretched. How much, then, must I be hated, I who am more miserable than any living thing? Even you, my creator, hate me and push me away, though I am your creature, tied to you by a bond that only the death of one of us can break. You want to kill me. How dare you play with life like this? Do your duty towards me, and I will do mine towards you and the rest of mankind. If you agree to my conditions, I will leave them and you in peace. If you refuse, I will feed the hungry mouth of death until it is full of the blood of the friends you have left.”

I could not bear it any longer. I sprang at him with all my strength. He stepped aside easily.

“Be calm!” he said. “Listen to me before you pour your hatred on my head. Haven't I suffered enough? Remember, you made me stronger than you. But I will not fight you. I am your creature. I ought to be your Adam, but instead I am the fallen angel, driven away from happiness for no crime at all. Everywhere I see joy, and I alone am shut out of it forever.”

He took a step towards me, and his voice softened.

“I was kind and good,” he said. “Misery made me a monster. Make me happy, and I will be good again.”

“Go away!” I cried. “I will not listen to you. There can be nothing between us. We are enemies.”

“How can I move you?” he said. “Believe me, Frankenstein, I was full of love for the world. My soul glowed with it. But I am alone, miserably alone. You, my creator, hate me. What hope do I have from other people, who owe me nothing? They push me away and hate me too. These empty mountains and frozen glaciers are my only home. The caves of ice, which I alone do not fear, are the only places where people do not chase me.”

Then he did something I did not expect. He raised his huge hand and placed it over my eyes, so that I could not see his face.

“There,” he said. “Now you are free from the sight you hate. Still, you can listen to me and grant me your pity. I ask you only this: hear my story. It is long and strange. Come to the hut on the mountain. The sun is still high. Before it goes down behind those snowy peaks, you will have heard everything, and you can decide. It depends on you whether I leave the world of men forever and live a harmless life, or become the terror of your kind and the cause of your own ruin.”

I hesitated. For the first time, I felt what the duty of a creator towards his creature might be. Shouldn't I at least listen before I judged him?

I followed him across the ice. The sky grew grey and a cold rain began to fall. We entered the hut, and he lit a fire. I sat down beside it, and the creature, sitting opposite me with his terrible face lit by the flames, began his story.

chapters.title: Chapter 6. The Creature's Story
chapters.text:
This is the story he told me, as nearly as I can remember his words.

I can hardly remember the first days of my life. I saw, felt, heard and smelled all at the same time. Light pressed on my eyes so strongly that I had to close them. Then darkness came, and I was afraid. When I left your room, I put on some clothes I found there and walked out into the night. I came to a forest near Ingolstadt. I was cold and hungry, and I sat down under a tree and cried.

Slowly I learned. I found berries to eat and drank from streams. I noticed the moon rising, and I could not stop looking at it. I heard the birds singing and tried to copy them, but the ugly sounds that came out of my throat frightened me into silence.

One day I found a fire that some beggars had left behind. I was delighted by its warmth and pushed my hand into the burning coals. I pulled it out again with a cry. How strange, I thought, that the same thing can give such pleasure and such pain!

When the forest could no longer feed me, I walked to a village. I had hardly put my foot inside one door when the children screamed and a woman fainted. Some ran away; others attacked me with stones and sticks until I fled, bruised and bleeding, into the open fields.

That night I found a low shed, built against the wall of a small cottage in the woods. Through a crack in the wall I could see into the cottage itself. This miserable shed became my home for almost a year.

In the cottage lived an old man, who was blind, and his two grown-up children, Felix and Agatha. Their family name was De Lacey. In the evenings the old man played the guitar, and his music was so sweet that tears came to my eyes. The young people treated their father with such tenderness that I felt a strange mixture of pain and joy.

They were poor, very poor. Sometimes the young people gave all their food to the old man and went hungry themselves. When I saw this, I stopped stealing from their store of food at night. Instead, I gathered wood in the forest and left it by their door. In the morning I heard them speak of a good spirit who was helping them. I was that good spirit, and I was proud.

I listened to them speak, and slowly I realised that their sounds had meanings. I learned the words for fire, milk, bread and wood. I learned what they called each other: father, sister, brother, Felix, Agatha. It was a godlike science, and I wanted it more than anything.

I admired the cottagers' beauty. Then one day I saw myself in a pool of clear water. At first I jumped back, unable to believe that the monster in the water was really me. When I understood, I was filled with the bitterest feelings of shame and despair.

In spring a young woman arrived on horseback. She was Safie, a beautiful Arabian girl whom Felix loved, and she did not speak their language. So Felix began to teach her, and I, hidden behind the wall, learned with her. I learned to speak, and then to read. Felix read history to her, and I heard about empires and wars, about rich men and poor men. I learned that people respect two things above all: noble birth and money. I had neither. I had no family, no name. And I was hideous.

What was I? The question returned again and again, and I could only answer it with groans.

One night in the forest I found a leather bag with three books inside: Paradise Lost, a volume of Plutarch's Lives and The Sorrows of Young Werther. Paradise Lost moved me most. Like Adam, I had been made by a creator, and I was connected to no other living being. But Adam came from the hands of God as a perfect, happy creature, protected by his maker. I was wretched, helpless and alone. Many times I thought that Satan was a better picture of my situation than Adam.

Then I looked at some papers I had found in the pocket of the coat I had taken from your room. They were pages from your journal, Frankenstein. You had written down every step of your work, and your disgust at what you were making. Now I could read. I learned everything.

“Cursed day when I received life!” I cried. “Cursed creator! Why did you form a monster so horrible that even you turned away from me in disgust? God made man beautiful, in his own image. But my form is a filthy copy of yours, more horrible because it is so like it. Satan had his companions, other devils, to admire him. But I am alone, and hated.”

And yet I still had hope. The cottagers were good and kind. If they could only see past my appearance, if they could know my heart, surely they would not turn me away? The old man was blind. He could not see my face. I would speak to him first, alone, and win his friendship.

I waited for the right day for months. At last it came.

chapters.title: Chapter 7. Fire and Revenge
chapters.text:
The creature went on with his story.

One autumn day, Felix, Agatha and Safie went out for a long walk. The old man was alone. My heart was pounding. I knocked on the door.

“Who is there?” said the old man. “Come in.”

I entered. “Forgive me,” I said. “I am a tired traveller. Could I sit by your fire for a few minutes?”

He welcomed me kindly, and as we talked, my courage grew. I told him I hoped to find some friends, people I loved but who had never seen me. “They are kind people,” I said, “but I am afraid that when they see me, they will see only a monster.”

“Don't despair,” said the old man. “The hearts of men, when they are not blinded by selfishness, are full of love. I am blind and cannot see your face, but your words tell me you are sincere. It would give me true pleasure to help you.”

At that moment I heard footsteps outside. I seized the old man's hand. “Now is the time!” I cried. “Save and protect me! You and your family are the friends I am looking for. Do not leave me in the hour of my need!”

“Great God!” said the old man. “Who are you?”

The door opened. Felix, Safie and Agatha came in. Agatha fainted, and Safie ran out. Felix rushed forward, tore me from his father, and struck me again and again with a stick. I could have torn him to pieces, as a lion tears an antelope. But my heart sank inside me like a stone, and I did not fight back. I escaped to my shed.

That night I raged through the forest like a wild beast. A few days later, the family left the cottage forever. Then I piled wood around the empty house and set fire to it. I watched it burn.

From that moment I declared war on all mankind, and above all on the man who had made me.

I knew from your papers that you lived in Geneva, so I set off south, travelling only at night. Once I saw a young girl fall into a fast river. I jumped in and pulled her out, but a man ran up, took her from my arms and shot me. That was my reward for kindness. The bullet broke my shoulder, and for weeks I lay in the forest, burning with pain and hatred.

Months later, I reached the fields near Geneva. One evening a beautiful little boy came running towards me. This child was too young to have learned to hate. If I could take him and teach him, I would have a companion in this empty world.

I caught him as he passed. As soon as he saw my face, he screamed.

“Let me go!” he cried. “Monster! Ugly wretch! You want to eat me! My papa is Monsieur Frankenstein. He'll punish you!”

“Frankenstein! Then you belong to my enemy, to the man I have sworn to take revenge on. You will be my first victim.”

I grasped his throat to silence him, and in a moment he lay dead at my feet.

I looked at my victim, and my heart swelled with a terrible joy. I, too, can create despair, I thought. This death will bring him misery.

Around his neck I saw a picture of a lovely woman. For a moment her gentle face softened me. Then I remembered that such a face would turn away from me in horror. I took the picture. Later, in a barn, I found a young woman asleep on the straw. I bent over her and put the picture into the pocket of her dress. She would be blamed, I thought. Let her pay for my crime.

He stopped and looked at me. “You know the rest, Frankenstein,” he said. “Now hear what I want. I am alone and miserable. Man will not live with me. But a woman as ugly as I am would not turn away from me. You must make a female for me, a companion with whom I can live. I demand it as my right.”

I stood up, shaking with anger.

“I refuse,” I said. “No torture will ever make me agree. Shall I create another like you, so that together you can destroy the world? Go! I have answered you.”

“You are wrong,” he replied calmly. “If any being felt kindness towards me, I would return it a hundred times. If you give me a companion, we will go to the wild lands of South America. We will eat acorns and berries. No man will ever see us again. We will live in peace, and I will die without cursing my maker.”

His words moved me. I thought of the stones thrown at him and the bullet in his shoulder. Perhaps I owed him this.

“I agree,” I said at last, “if you swear to leave Europe forever as soon as I give her to you.”

“I swear it,” he cried, “by the sun and the blue sky of heaven! Go home and begin your work. I will watch your progress, and when you are ready, I will appear.”

Then he turned and ran down the mountain, faster than an eagle flies, and was lost among the waves of the sea of ice.

chapters.title: Chapter 8. The Broken Promise
chapters.text:
I came down from the mountain a changed man. Weeks passed, then months, and I could not bring myself to begin. Every time I thought of the work, my whole body filled with disgust.

One day my father took me aside. “Victor,” he said gently, “do you still love Elizabeth? Do you still want to marry her? Perhaps you think of her only as a sister.”

“I love her with all my heart,” I said. “Nothing would make me happier.”

But I could not marry her while this terrible duty hung over me. I needed to finish the work first, and I could not do it in my father's house. I had heard that some English scientists had made discoveries that would help me. So I told my father that I wanted to travel to England before the wedding, and he agreed. To my great joy, Henry Clerval was to come with me.

We sailed down the Rhine past castles and vineyards, and Henry's delight in everything was like sunshine. I tried to share his happiness, but a black cloud never left me. Even as I smiled at him, I imagined the creature following us, watching from the hills.

We spent the winter in London and travelled north through Oxford to Scotland. There I left Henry with friends and went on alone. I chose a remote island in the Orkneys, a bare rock beaten by the waves, where only five people lived, and set up my laboratory in a small hut.

In Ingolstadt I had worked with passion. Now I worked with cold horror, and my heart often sickened at the work of my hands.

One evening, three years after that night in November, I was sitting in my laboratory. The moon was rising from the sea, and I had almost finished. Then a new thought came into my head.

What was I doing? The first creature had promised to leave Europe, but the female had promised nothing. She might be ten thousand times more evil than her mate. She might refuse the agreement made before her creation. They might hate each other. And even if they went to the wild lands of the New World as he had promised, they might have children. A race of devils might spread over the earth and make the life of mankind full of terror. Did I have the right, for my own peace, to bring this curse on all future generations?

I trembled, and when I looked up, I saw him. By the light of the moon, the creature was standing at the window. A ghastly grin wrinkled his lips as he watched me. He had followed me all this way to see the work completed.

I looked at his face, so full of evil and cunning, and I felt like a madman. In front of his eyes I tore the thing I had been making into pieces.

The wretch watched me destroy the creature on whom he had built all his hopes. With a howl of devilish despair and revenge, he disappeared.

Some hours later, the door opened, and he stood in front of me.

“You have destroyed the work you began,” he said in a hollow voice. “What do you mean by it? Do you dare to break your promise? I have suffered cold and hunger. I followed you down the Rhine and among the islands of Scotland. And now you destroy my only hope?”

“Go!” I said. “I do break my promise. I will never create another like you.”

“Slave,” he said, “I reasoned with you before, but you have shown that you do not deserve my patience. Remember that I have power. You think you are miserable, but I can make you so wretched that the light of day will be hateful to you. You are my creator, but I am your master. Obey!”

“Your threats cannot make me do an evil thing,” I answered. “Leave me. I am firm.”

“Very well,” he said. “I will go. But remember: I will be with you on your wedding night.”

I rushed at him, but he escaped and jumped into his boat, which shot across the waters like an arrow.

Late the next night, I put the remains of my work into a basket with heavy stones, rowed out to sea and threw it into the dark water. Then I lay down in the boat, and the sound of the waves sent me to sleep.

When I woke, the sun was high, and a strong wind had carried me far from the island. At last, as evening came, I saw land and steered towards a small harbour. Some people on the shore looked at me strangely.

“My good friends,” I said, “would you tell me the name of this town?”

“You will know that soon enough,” a man replied roughly. “You are in Ireland. And you will have to come with us to see Mr Kirwin, the magistrate, to give an account of the death of a gentleman who was found murdered here last night.”

They took me to a room where a body lay on a table. I walked towards it calmly, believing I had nothing to fear. Then I looked at the face.

It was Henry Clerval. On his neck I saw the black marks of fingers.

chapters.title: Chapter 9. The Wedding Night
chapters.text:
The sight of Henry's body threw me into a violent fever. For two months I lay in an Irish prison, close to death, crying out in my sleep that I was the murderer of William, of Justine and of Clerval.

When I woke at last, the magistrate, Mr Kirwin, was sitting beside my bed. He was a kind old man, and he had written to my father. A few days later my father himself came into my cell. I held out my arms to him.

“Are you safe?” I cried. “And Elizabeth? And Ernest?”

My father calmed me and assured me that they were well. In time, witnesses proved that I had been on the Orkney Islands when Henry was killed, and I was set free. My father took me home, a ruined and broken man.

At home, Elizabeth welcomed me with tears. She had grown thin, and some of the brightness had gone from her eyes, but her gentleness was the same. My father wished to see us married as soon as possible, and I agreed. The creature's words were always in my mind: “I will be with you on your wedding night.” I believed that he meant to kill me on that night. Very well, I thought. Let him come. One of us would die, and either way I would be free. I carried pistols and a dagger with me everywhere, and I watched constantly for him.

Elizabeth saw how anxious I was. “Something is troubling you, Victor,” she said quietly. “Tell me.”

“I have one terrible secret,” I answered. “I will tell you the day after our wedding. Until then, please don't ask me.”

We were married in the spring. After the ceremony we set off by boat across the lake for the town of Evian, where we were to spend our first night. The day was beautiful. The sun shone, the mountains rose white above the blue water, and Elizabeth's hand was in mine. Those were the last moments of my life in which I knew happiness.

We reached the inn at eight o'clock, as the sun set. Soon the wind rose from the west, and heavy rain began to fall. As night came on, a thousand fears filled my mind. I walked up and down the passages of the inn, my hand on the pistol in my coat, examining every corner where my enemy might hide.

Elizabeth watched me in silence. “What is it, Victor?” she asked at last. “What are you afraid of?”

“Be calm, my love,” I said. “Only this night, and all will be safe. But this night is dreadful, very dreadful.”

I begged her to go to bed, and I promised to join her soon. I wanted to find the creature before he could find me.

She left me. I continued walking through the inn, searching. Then I heard a shrill and terrible scream. It came from our room.

As I heard it, the whole truth rushed into my mind. My arms dropped, and every muscle in my body froze. Then I ran.

She was there, lifeless, lying across the bed, her head hanging down and her pale face half covered by her hair. The murderous mark of the creature's grasp was on her neck. Even now, wherever I look, I see that picture: her bloodless arms, and her body thrown across her wedding bed by the murderer.

I fell senseless on the floor. When I came to myself, the people of the inn were all around me. I ran back to her and held her in my arms, but the cold of death was already in her.

Then I looked up. The shutters had been thrown back, and at the open window, in the pale yellow light of the moon, I saw the most hideous and hateful figure. A grin was on the monster's face. He seemed to mock me as he pointed with his devilish finger towards the body of my wife.

I took out my pistol and fired. He escaped, ran as fast as lightning and plunged into the lake.

My father did not survive the news. Elizabeth had been like his own daughter, and the grief was too much for his old heart. A few days later he died in my arms.

What happened to me after that, I do not know. For many months I lay in a cell, chained, they told me, because I was mad. When at last I recovered my reason, I had only one thought left: revenge.

I went to a magistrate in Geneva and told him everything. He listened politely, but I could see that he did not believe me, or believed that no one could ever catch such a creature. I left him in a fury.

I decided to leave Geneva forever. On my last night, I went to the cemetery where William, Elizabeth and my father lay. I knelt on the grass and swore by the spirits of the dead that I would hunt down the demon until one of us was destroyed.

As I finished, a loud, devilish laugh rang through the night. It seemed to echo from the mountains all around me. Then a voice, which I knew too well, whispered close to my ear:

“I am satisfied, miserable wretch! You have decided to live, and I am satisfied.”

chapters.title: Chapter 10. Lost in Darkness and Distance
chapters.text:
So the chase began. I followed him down the Rhône to the Mediterranean. He hid on a ship bound for the Black Sea, and I followed him there, and then across the wild lands of Tartary and Russia. Sometimes he left messages for me, cut into the bark of trees.

“My reign is not yet over,” one of them said. “You live, and my power is complete. Follow me. I am going to the everlasting ice of the north, where you will feel the misery of cold and frost, which I do not feel. You will find a dead hare near this place. Eat it and get your strength back. Come on, my enemy. We have yet to fight for our lives.”

He was keeping me alive so that I would suffer. And I, God forgive me, was glad of his food.

When the snow came, I bought a sledge and dogs. At last, from the top of a hill of ice, I saw him, less than a mile ahead. But then the sea roared beneath me, the ice cracked and split, and I was left floating on a broken piece while he disappeared. That was how you found me, Walton.

And now I have one last thing to ask of you. If I die before he does, swear that you will find him and kill him. Do not let him live to add to his crimes.

26th August.

Here his story ended, Margaret. I believe every word, because I saw the giant with my own eyes.

2nd September.

We are still surrounded by mountains of ice, which may crush our ship at any moment. Several of my men have already died of cold. Frankenstein is growing weaker every day.

5th September.

Today some of my sailors came into my cabin and demanded that, if the ice opens, we turn back to England. Frankenstein raised himself in his bed.

“What do you mean?” he said. “Did you not call this a glorious expedition? Glorious because it was dangerous. And now, at the first sight of danger, you want to go home like cowards! Be men, or be more than men. This ice is not as strong as your hearts can be. It will break if you say that it must.”

The men were moved, but they did not change their minds. And I could not lead them all to their deaths for the sake of my dream. I have agreed. If the ice lets us go, we will sail south.

12th September.

It is over. I have lost my hopes of glory, and I have lost my friend.

When I told Frankenstein that we were turning back, he tried to stand, but he was too weak.

“Farewell, Walton,” he said. “Look for happiness in a quiet life, and avoid ambition, even the apparently innocent ambition of making a name in science. And yet, why do I say this? I have been destroyed by these hopes, but another man may succeed.”

His voice grew fainter, and a gentle smile appeared on his lips. Then his eyes closed forever.

It is midnight. A few minutes ago I heard a sound from the cabin where his body lies, a voice like a groan. I went in. Over the coffin stood a figure of gigantic size, and one vast hand stretched out over the body. As I entered, he turned towards the window. I had never seen anything so horrible as that face.

“That is also my victim!” he cried. “Oh, Frankenstein! What use is it now to ask your forgiveness? I destroyed you by destroying everyone you loved. And now you are cold, and you cannot answer me.”

At last I found my voice. “It is too late to feel sorry,” I said. “If you had listened to your conscience earlier, Frankenstein would still be alive.”

“Do you think I felt no pain?” he answered. “He suffered, but not the ten-thousandth part of what I suffered. My heart was made for love and sympathy. When it was turned by misery to hatred, the change cost me more torture than you can imagine. After Clerval died, I pitied Frankenstein, and I hated myself. But when I learned that he was going to marry, and hoped for the happiness I could never have, envy and bitterness filled me. I was the slave, not the master, of what I had become.

“You hate me, but you cannot hate me more than I hate myself. Everyone has sinned against me, it is true. But I am the one who killed the innocent and the helpless. I killed my creator, the best of men. And now he is gone, and I am alone.

“My work is nearly finished. I will leave your ship on this raft of ice and go to the most northern end of the earth. I will build my own funeral fire and burn this miserable body to ashes, so that no curious, unhappy man may ever make another like me. I will no longer see the sun or the stars, or feel the wind on my face. Soon I will die, and what I now feel will be felt no more. Farewell!”

As he said this, he jumped from the cabin window onto the raft of ice that lay close to the ship. He was soon carried away by the waves and lost in darkness and distance.
